Also called ''aller-trout''.

¶
'''allette''', ''n.'' See ''alette.''

'''alleve†''', ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. spelled ''aleive''; < OF. ''allever'', ''alever'', < L. ''allevare'', ''adlevare'', lift up, raise, lighten, alleviate, < ''ad'', to, + ''levare'', lift up, lighten: see ''alleviate'', and cf. ''relieve''.] To alleviate; relieve. ''Surrey.''

'''allevement†''', ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''aleavement''; < ''alleve'' + ''-ment''.] The act of alleviating or relieving; alleviation.

'''alleviate''' (a-lē′vi-āt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''alleviated'', ppr. ''alleviating''. [< LL. ''alleviatus'', pp. of ''alleviare'', ''adleviare'', for L. ''allevare'', ''adlevare'', lighten, alleviate, < ''ad'', to, + ''levare'', lift up, lighten, < ''levis'', light, not heavy: see ''levity''. Cf. ''allege''<sup>2</sup> and ''alleve''.] '''1.''' To make light, in a figurative sense; remove in part; lessen, mitigate, or make easier to be endured: as, to ''alleviate'' sorrow, pain, care, punishment, burdens, etc.: opposed to ''aggravate''.
{{smaller block|Excellent medicines to ''alleviate'' those evils which we bring upon ourselves.
{{right|''Bentley.''}}
The darkest complexion is not a little ''alleviated'' by a black hood.
{{right|''Addison.''}}
The little apples which it [the nebbak-tree] bears are slightly acid and excellent for ''alleviating'' thirst.
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Lands of the Saracen, p. 69.}}}}
'''2.''' To represent as less; lessen the magnitude or heinousness of; extenuate: applied to moral conduct: as, to ''alleviate'' an offense. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He ''alleviates'' his fault by an excuse.
{{right|''Johnson.''}}}}

='''Syn.''' Mitigation, palliation, relief.

'''alleviative''' (a-lē′vi-ā-tiv), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''alleviate'' + ''-ive.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' Tending to alleviate or mitigate.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which alleviates or mitigates: as, “some cheering ''alleviative,''” ''Corah’s Doom'' (1672), p. 176.

Also spelled ''ally''.

¶
'''alleyed''' (al′id), ''a.'' Laid out as an alley, or with alleys.
{{smaller block|<poem>Untrimmed, undressed, neglected now
Was ''alleyed'' walk and orchard bough.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, ii. 17.}}}}

'''alley-taw''' (al′i-tâ), ''n.'' [< ''alley''<sup>2</sup> + ''taw''<sup>2</sup>.] An alley; a large playing-marble. Sometimes written ''alley-tor'', as vulgarly pronounced.
{{smaller block|After inquiring whether he had won any ''alley-tors'' or commoneys lately, he made use of this expression.
{{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick.}}}}

'''alleyway''' (al′i-wā), ''n.'' A short alley; a lane or narrow passage of small extent, as between two houses.
{{smaller block|By substantial walls of adobe, with narrow ''alleyways'' running between.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXV. 81.}}}}

'''All-father''' (âl′fä″ᴛ̵ʜėr), ''n.'' [< ''all'', orig. gen. pl., + ''father''; after Icel. ''Alfödhr''.] The Father of all: a name originally of Odin, now sometimes applied to Jupiter and to God.
{{smaller block|<poem>And I told of the good ''All-father''
Who cares for us here below.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', First Snowfall.}}}}

'''all-fired''' (âl-fīrd′), ''a.'' [Said to be a euphemism for ''hell-fired'', and hence defined as ‘infernal,’ but prob. to be taken at its face value: < ''all'' + ''fire'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>, ''all'' intensifying the merely rhetorical ''fire''.] Tremendous: as, an ''all-fired'' noise; he was in an ''all-fired'' rage. [Colloq.]

'''all-fours''' (âl-fōrz′), ''n.'' A game of cards played
readings.c2s3:
{{smaller|by from two to six persons with hands of six cards each, dealt from a full pack, the top one of the remaining cards being turned as the trump, and the cards ranking as in whist.}} {{smaller|It derives its name from the four chances of which it consists, for each of which a point is scored. These chances are the securing of ''high'', or the ace of trumps or next best trump out; of ''low'', or the deuce of trumps or next lowest trump out; of ''jack'', or the knave of trumps; of ''game'', or tricks containing cards which will make the largest sum when added together, an ace being counted as four, a king as three, a queen as two, a jack as one, and a ten-spot as ten, the other cards not counting. The player who has all these is said to have ''all-fours''. Also called ''old sledge'', ''seven-up'', and ''high-low-jack''.}}

'''allgood''' (âl′gu̇d), ''n.'' An old name of the plant Good Henry, or English mercury, ''Chenopodium Bonus-Henricus''.

'''all-hail''' (âl-hāl′), ''v. t.'' [See ''hail''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.''] To salute or address with the exclamation ''all hail!'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Who ''all-hailed'' me, Thane of Cawdor.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 5.}}}}

'''All-hallon†''', '''All-hallond†''', etc. Same as ''All-hallows''.

'''All-hallow''' (âl-hal′ō), ''n.'' See ''All-hallows''.

'''Allhallowe’en''' (âl-hal′ọ̄-ēn), ''n.'' [For ''Allhallow-even'': but see ''All-hallows''.] See ''All-hallows'' and ''Hallowe’en''.

'''Allhallowmas''' (âl-hal′ọ̄-mas), ''n.'' [< ME. ''alhalowmesse'', ''alhalwemesse'', < AS. ''ealra hālgena mæsse-dæg'', all saints’ mass-day: see ''All-hallows''.] Allhallow-tide.

'''All-hallown†''' (âl-hal′ōn), ''n.'' [Also corruptly ''Allhallon'', ''-hollon'', ''-hollan'', ''-holland'', < ME. ''al halowen'', < AS. ''ealle hālgan'', all saints: see ''All-''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|allenarly|147|alliance}}</noinclude>only, < ''ane'', one: see ''anerly''. Cf. ME. ''all-oneli'', ''alle-oneli'', ''all-anly'', only, lit. all only: see ''all'' and ''only''.] Only; solely; merely: a technical word used in Scotch conveyancing. {{smaller|Thus, where lands are conveyed to a father, “for his life-rent use ''allenarly'',” the force of the expression is that the father’s right is restricted to a mere life-rent, or at best to a fiduciary fee, even in circumstances where, but for the word ''allenarly'', the father would have been unlimited fiar.}}

'''aller<sup>1</sup>''' (âl′ėr), ''n.''  [E. dial., < ME. ''aller'', < AS. ''alr'': see ''alder''<sup>1</sup>.]  Same as ''alder''<sup>1</sup>. [Prov. Eng.]

'''aller<sup>2</sup>†''', ''a.'' See ''alder''<sup>3</sup>.

'''aller-float''' (âl′ėr-flōt), ''n.''  [< ''aller''<sup>1</sup>, dial. form of ''alder''<sup>1</sup>, + ''float''.]  A local English name of a large trout of the common species, given from the fact that it hides under the roots of the alder, or is in season when the alder is budding. Also called ''aller-trout''.

'''allerion''' (a-lē′ri-ọn), ''n.''  [More correctly ''alerion'', < OF. ''alerion'', ''aleiron'' (F. ''alérion''), < ML. {{img float|file=century v01 p0173 c1f1.png|width=92px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Allerion.}}}} ''alario(n-)'', in her. a little eagle without beak or claws, in form suggesting L. ''alarius'', < ''ala'', a wing (see ''aisle''), but prob. of other origin; perhaps ult. < MHG. ''adelar'', G. ''adler'', an eagle.]  In ''her.'': (''a'') A bearing representing an eagle or eaglet displayed without feet or beak. (''b'') More rarely, an eagle heraldically represented, but complete.  ''Boutell.''

'''aller-trout''' (âl′ėr-trout), ''n.'' Same as ''aller-float''.

'''allette''', ''n.'' See ''alette.''

'''alleve†''', ''v. t.''  [Early mod. E. spelled ''aleive''; < OF. ''allever'', ''alever'', < L. ''allevare'', ''adlevare'', lift up, raise, lighten, alleviate, < ''ad'', to, + ''levare'', lift up, lighten: see ''alleviate'', and cf. ''relieve''.]  To alleviate; relieve.  ''Surrey.''

'''allevement†''', ''n.''  [Early mod. E. ''aleavement''; < ''alleve'' + ''-ment''.]  The act of alleviating or relieving; alleviation.

'''alleviate''' (a-lē′vi-āt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''alleviated'', ppr. ''alleviating''.  [< LL. ''alleviatus'', pp. of ''alleviare'', ''adleviare'', for L. ''allevare'', ''adlevare'', lighten, alleviate, < ''ad'', to, + ''levare'', lift up, lighten, < ''levis'', light, not heavy: see ''levity''. Cf. ''allege''<sup>2</sup> and ''alleve''.]  '''1.''' To make light, in a figurative sense; remove in part; lessen, mitigate, or make easier to be endured: as, to ''alleviate'' sorrow, pain, care, punishment, burdens, etc.: opposed to ''aggravate''.
{{smaller block|Excellent medicines to ''alleviate'' those evils which we bring upon ourselves.
{{right|''Bentley.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The darkest complexion is not a little ''alleviated'' by a black hood.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The little apples which it [the nebbak-tree] bears are slightly acid and excellent for ''alleviating'' thirst.
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Lands of the Saracen, p. 69.}}}}
'''2.''' To represent as less; lessen the magnitude or heinousness of; extenuate: applied to moral conduct: as, to ''alleviate'' an offense. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He ''alleviates'' his fault by an excuse.
{{right|''Johnson.''}}}}

='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Alleviate'', ''Relieve'', ''Mitigate'', ''Assuage'', ''Allay'', diminish, soften, abate, qualify, reduce. See ''allay''<sup>1</sup>. Where these words are applied to pain, etc., ''alleviate'' is to lighten somewhat, and especially in a soothing way; ''relieve'' and ''allay'' go further than ''alleviate'', removing in large measure or altogether. ''Mitigate'' is to make mild, less severe; perhaps it stands midway between ''alleviate'' and ''relieve''. ''Assuage'' is to calm down, and that idea underlies all its uses; ''allay'' conveys similarly the idea of putting to rest.}}
{{smaller block|To ''alleviate'' the congestion of the optic nerve and retina, the artificial leech should be applied several times at intervals of a few days, but should then be desisted from if no benefit results.
{{right|''J. S. Wells'', Dis. of Eye, p. 383.}}}}
{{smaller block|It [electricity] has ''relieved'' the paroxysms of angina pectoris.
{{right|''Quain'', Med. Dict., p. 430.}}}}
{{smaller block|In the advance of civilisation, there is a constant tendency to ''mitigate'' the severity of penal codes.
{{right|''Lecky'', Rationalism, I. 337.}}}}
{{smaller block|Foment the bruises, and the pains ''assuage''.
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., l. 2003.}}}}

'''alleviation''' (a-lē-vi-ā′shọn), ''n.''  [< ML. ''alleviatio(n-)'', L. ''allĕvatio(n-)'', < ''allevare'', lighten: see ''alleviate''.]  '''1.''' The act of alleviating. {{smaller|(''a'') The act of removing in part, lessening, mitigating, or making easier to be endured: as, the ''alleviation'' of taxes. (''b'') The act of making less by representation; extenuation: as, “''alleviations'' of faults,” ''South''.}} —'''2.''' That which lessens, mitigates, or makes more tolerable: as, the sympathy of a friend is an ''alleviation'' of grief.
{{smaller block|I have not wanted such ''alleviations'' of life as friendship could supply.
{{right|''Johnson''.}}}}
{{smaller block|His sister was waiting in a state of wondering alarm, which was not without its ''alleviations''.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 8.}}}}

='''Syn.''' Mitigation, palliation, relief.

'''alleviative''' (a-lē′vi-ā-tiv), ''a.'' and ''n.''  [< ''alleviate'' + ''-ive.'']  '''I.''' ''a.'' Tending to alleviate or mitigate.

'''II.''' ''n.'' That which alleviates or mitigates: as, “some cheering ''alleviative,''” ''Corah’s Doom'' (1672), p. 176.

'''alleviator''' (a-lē′vi-ā-tor), ''n.'' One who or that which alleviates, lightens, or mitigates.

'''alleviatory''' (a-lē′vi-ā-tō-ri), ''a.'' Fitted to alleviate; having the quality of alleviating.

'''allex''' (al′eks), ''n.''  [L., also ''hallex'', NL. ''hallux'': see ''hallux''.]  Same as ''hallux''. [Rare.]

'''alley<sup>1</sup>''' (al′i), ''n.''  [< ME. ''alei'', ''aley'', < OF. ''alee'' (F. ''allée''), a going, gallery, passage, < ''aler'', ''aller'' (F. ''aller''), go, var. of an earlier ''aner'' = Pr. ''anar'' = Cat. ''anar'' = Sp. Pg. ''andar'' = It. ''andare'', dial. ''anare'', go; of uncertain origin: either (1) < L. ''annare'', ''adnare'', swim to, toward, or along; in Cicero once used in sense of ‘come to, approach’; < ''ad'', to, + ''nare'', swim (see ''natation''); or (2) ult. < ML. *''anditare'' for L. ''aditare'' (cf. ML. ''anditus'' for L. ''aditus'', and ML. ''rendere'' for L. ''reddere'': see ''adit'' and ''render''), go to or approach often, freq. of ''adire'', pp. ''aditus'', go to, < ''ad'', to, + ''ire'', go: see ''adit''.]  A passage; especially, a narrow passage. {{smaller|(''a'') A passage in a building, giving access from one part to another; also sometimes used for ''aisle''. (''b'') A long, narrow inclosure with a smooth wooden floor for playing at bowls, skittles, etc. (''c'') A walk, inclosed with hedges or shrubbery, in a garden: as, “yonder ''alleys'' green,” ''Milton'', P. L., iv. 626.}}
{{smaller block|So long about the ''aleys'' is he goen.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Merchant’s Tale, l. 1080.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') A narrow passage or way in a town, as distinct from a public street. (''e'') In a printing-office, the space between two rows of composing-stands, in which compositors work at the cases on the stands.}}

'''alley<sup>2</sup>''' (al′i), ''n.''  [Said to be a contr. of ''alabaster'', from which alleys are said to have been made.]  A choice taw or large playing-marble. Also spelled ''ally''.

'''alleyed''' (al′id), ''a.'' Laid out as an alley, or with alleys.
{{smaller block|<poem>Untrimmed, undressed, neglected now
Was ''alleyed'' walk and orchard bough.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, ii. 17.}}}}

'''alley-taw''' (al′i-tâ), ''n.''  [< ''alley''<sup>2</sup> + ''taw''<sup>2</sup>.]  An alley; a large playing-marble. Sometimes written ''alley-tor'', as vulgarly pronounced.
{{smaller block|After inquiring whether he had won any ''alley-tors'' or commoneys lately, he made use of this expression.
{{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick.}}}}

'''alleyway''' (al′i-wā), ''n.'' A short alley; a lane or narrow passage of small extent, as between two houses.
{{smaller block|By substantial walls of adobe, with narrow ''alleyways'' running between.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXV. 81.}}}}

'''All-father''' (âl′fä″ᴛ̵ʜėr), ''n.''  [< ''all'', orig. gen. pl., + ''father''; after Icel. ''Alfödhr''.]  The Father of all: a name originally of Odin, now sometimes applied to Jupiter and to God.
{{smaller block|<poem>And I told of the good ''All-father''
Who cares for us here below.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', First Snowfall.}}}}

'''all-fired''' (âl-fīrd′), ''a.''  [Said to be a euphemism for ''hell-fired'', and hence defined as ‘infernal,’ but prob. to be taken at its face value: < ''all'' + ''fire'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>, ''all'' intensifying the merely rhetorical ''fire''.]  Tremendous: as, an ''all-fired'' noise; he was in an ''all-fired'' rage. [Colloq.]

'''all-fours''' (âl-fōrz′), ''n.'' A game of cards played {{smaller|by from two to six persons with hands of six cards each, dealt from a full pack, the top one of the remaining cards being turned as the trump, and the cards ranking as in whist.}} {{smaller|It derives its name from the four chances of which it consists, for each of which a point is scored. These chances are the securing of ''high'', or the ace of trumps or next best trump out; of ''low'', or the deuce of trumps or next lowest trump out; of ''jack'', or the knave of trumps; of ''game'', or tricks containing cards which will make the largest sum when added together, an ace being counted as four, a king as three, a queen as two, a jack as one, and a ten-spot as ten, the other cards not counting. The player who has all these is said to have ''all-fours''. Also called ''old sledge'', ''seven-up'', and ''high-low-jack''.}}

'''allgood''' (âl′gu̇d), ''n.'' An old name of the plant Good Henry, or English mercury, ''Chenopodium Bonus-Henricus''.

'''all-hail''' (âl-hāl′), ''v. t.''  [See ''hail''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'']  To salute or address with the exclamation ''all hail!'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Who ''all-hailed'' me, Thane of Cawdor.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 5.}}}}

'''All-hallon†''', '''All-hallond†''', etc. Same as ''All-hallows''.

'''All-hallow''' (âl-hal′ō), ''n.'' See ''All-hallows''.

'''Allhallowe’en''' (âl-hal′ọ̄-ēn), ''n.''  [For ''Allhallow-even'': but see ''All-hallows''.]  See ''All-hallows'' and ''Hallowe’en''.

'''Allhallowmas''' (âl-hal′ọ̄-mas), ''n.''  [< ME. ''alhalowmesse'', ''alhalwemesse'', < AS. ''ealra hālgena mæsse-dæg'', all saints’ mass-day: see ''All-hallows''.]  Allhallow-tide.

'''All-hallown†''' (âl-hal′ōn), ''n.''  [Also corruptly ''Allhallon'', ''-hollon'', ''-hollan'', ''-holland'', < ME. ''al halowen'', < AS. ''ealle hālgan'', all saints: see ''Allhallows''.'']  Same as ''All-hallows.''—'''All-hallown summer''', {{smaller|formerly the name in England of a season of fine weather in the late autumn, corresponding to St. Martin’s summer in France and to Indian summer in the United States. ''N. E. D.''}}
{{smaller block|Farewell, the latter spring! Farewell, ''All-hallown summer!''
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 2.}}}}

'''All-hallows, All-hallow''' (âl-hal′ōz, -ō), ''n.''  [Prop. ''All-hallows'', pl., but in comp. ''All-hallow'' (sc. ''day'', ''eve'', ''mass'', ''summer'', ''tide''); in early mod. E. and dial. also ''All-hallown'', ''-hallon'', ''-hallan'', ''-hollon'', ''-hollan'', ''-holland'', etc.; < ME. ''al halowes'', earlier ''al halowen'', < AS. ''ealle hālgan'', all hallows, i. e., all saints (see ''all'' and ''hallow''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''), usually in gen. pl. ''ealra hālgena'', ME. ''alre'' (or ''alle'') ''halowene'', ''halewune'', etc., (day, tide, feast, etc.) of all hallows. The term. ''-n'', corruptly ''-nd'', thus represents the AS. pl. suffix ''-an'', and in comp. the gen. pl. ''-ena'', the latter, ME. ''-ene'', being appar. merged in ''e’en'' in ''Allhallowe’en'', q. v.]  '''1.''' All saints. It was formerly common to dedicate a church to ''All-hallows.''—'''2.''' All Saints’ day, the 1st of November: a feast dedicated to all the saints in general. See ''All Saints’ day'', under ''saint''.

'''Allhallow-tide''' (âl-hal′ō-tīd), ''n.''  [Early mod. E. also ''Allhallown-tide'', ''Alhallon-tyd'', ''Allhollon-tide'', etc.: see ''All-hallows'', ''All-hallown'', and ''tide''.]  The time near All Saints’ day, November 1. Also called ''Hallow-tide''.
{{smaller block|Apples, pears, hawthorn-quicks, oaks, set them at ''All-hollon-tide'', and command them to prosper; set them at Candlemas, and intreat them to grow.
{{right|''Ray'', Eng. Proverbs (1678), p. 350.}}}}

'''allheal''' (âl′hēl), ''n.''  [< ''all'' + ''heal''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''panacea'' and ''Panax.'']  The name of a plant, cat’s valerian, ''Valeriana officinalis.'' The clown’s allheal, or clown’s woundwort, is ''Stachys palustris.''

'''alliable''' (a̤-lī′a̤-bl), ''a.''  [< ''ally''<sup>1</sup> + ''-able.'']  Capable of forming or of entering into an alliance.

'''alliaceous''' (al-i-ā′shius), ''a.''  [< L. ''allium,'' garlic, + ''-aceous.'' See ''Allium.'']  '''1.''' Pertaining to or having the properties of the genus ''Allium,'' which includes the onion and garlic.—'''2.''' Having the peculiar smell or taste of the onion: applied specifically to minerals which contain arsenic and emit a garlic-like odor when heated on charcoal before the blowpipe.

'''alliance''' (a̤-lī′ans), ''n.''  [< ME. ''aliance, aliaunce,'' < OF. ''aliance,'' < ML. ''alligantia,'' < ''alligare'' (OF. ''alier''), ally, bind to: see ''ally''<sup>1</sup> and ''-ance.'']  '''1.''' The state of being allied or connected; the relation between parties allied or connected. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') Marriage, or the relation or union brought about between families through marriage.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And great ''alliances'' but useless prove
To one that comes herself from mighty Jove.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden,'' Helen to Paris, l. 55.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Connection by kindred. [Rare.]}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For my father’s sake, . . .
And for ''alliance’'' sake.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' 1 Hen. VI., ii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller|(''c'') Union between nations, contracted by compact, treaty, or league. Such alliance may be ''defensive,'' that is, an agreement to defend each other when attacked; or ''offensive,'' that is, an agreement to make a combined attack on another nation; or it may be both offensive and defensive.}}
{{smaller block|An ''alliance'' was accordingly formed by Austria with England and Holland against France.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.,'' III. 126.}}}}
{{smaller|(''d'') A joining of efforts or interests by persons, families, states, or organizations: as, an ''alliance'' between church}} and state.

{{smaller block|An intimate ''alliance'' was formed between the Arian kings and the Arian clergy. {{right|''Buckle'', Civilization, II. ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Lydgate . . . had . . . the conviction that the medical profession . . . offered the most direct ''alliance'' between intellectual conquest and the social good. {{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, I. 159.}}}}

'''2.''' The compact or treaty which is the instrument of allying or confederating: as, to draw up an ''alliance''.—'''3.''' The aggregate of persons or parties allied.

<poem>Therefore, let our ''alliance'' be combin’d.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 1.}}

'''4.''' In ''bot.'', a grade intermediate between class and order: the equivalent in Lindley’s classification of the more recent term ''cohort''.—'''5.''' In ''zoöl.'', a natural group of related families; a superfamily or suborder.—{{smaller|'''Arms of alliance''', in ''her.'', arms which are obtained through matrimonial alliances.—'''Evangelical Alliance.''' See ''evangelical''.—'''Holy Alliance.''' See ''holy''.='''Syn.''' ''Alliance'', ''League'', ''Confederacy'', ''Coalition'', relationship, affinity, combination, federation, copartnership. The first four words have been used without distinction to express the union or coöperation of two or more persons, organizations, or states. ''Alliance'' is the most general term. Often a ''confederacy'' and sometimes a ''league'' between states means a closer union than an ''alliance''. ''Alliance'' is rarely used of a combination for evil; but the other words are often so used, ''confederacy'' having specifically such a meaning in law. ''Alliance'' alone is used of the union of families by marriage. ''Coalition'' is often used of the temporary coöperation of persons, parties, or states that are ordinarily opposed.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
